item.title: Two Open-Source RoboCup Stacks on One Small Humanoid: B-Human vs HTWK on the Booster K1
item.description:
The Booster K1 is a small humanoid that many RoboCup teams now use. Two of the strongest teams have published software that can run on it, and they took very different paths.

  • HTWK (Leipzig) published HTWK Gym, a reinforcement learning framework for training walking policies for the Booster T1 and K1. You bring the rest of the soccer stack.
  • B-Human (Bremen) published its 2026 code release: a complete robot soccer program, perception to motion, now for the K1 and T1 only.

I have been working with both this autumn. My K1 work started on the HTWK route: a walking policy trained in HTWK Gym, connected through a bridge to a ROS 2 behavior-tree soccer stack. This week I also installed the B-Human release on a K1. This post compares the two, as architecture. It is not a benchmark. Neither is “better”. They answer different questions.

Shape: one program versus many nodes

B-Human is one C++ program, about 150,000 lines. Vision, localization, behavior and motion all live inside it, in threads: camera, motion at 500 Hz, audio, cognition, debug. All motions are RL policies: walk, kick and get-up, running at 50 Hz through ONNX Runtime.

The HTWK route is a set of pieces. HTWK Gym trains a 12-output lower-body walking policy (ParameterWalk, 54 inputs). On the robot, a bridge runs that policy next to separate ROS 2 nodes for vision and behavior. Get-up and other skills stay with the Booster firmware.

The trade-off is the usual one. One program is easier to make consistent: one clock, one set of frames, one place to debug. Separate nodes are easier to swap and to mix with the vendor’s own stack, but every boundary is a place where timing and ownership can go wrong.

Who owns the robot

This was the biggest difference for me.

B-Human never gives control back to the vendor during play. It runs the whole time in Booster’s CUSTOM mode. Its own “prepare” and “walk” are states inside CUSTOM, not Booster’s PREP and WALK. A parent watchdog process starts the control program. If the control program dies, the watchdog switches the robot to damping and saves a trace. The emergency button (F1) is always handled by the watchdog, so it still works when the control program misbehaves. No robot data for 50 ms counts as an emergency.

The HTWK route leans on the firmware. The firmware’s standing posture is the safe home. The bridge hands over from firmware to the RL policy, and hands back to the firmware’s PREP mode when it releases. I wrote about that handover in the motion owner post.

Both models end in the same place on a fault: damping. And damping drops a standing robot in either stack. That is worth remembering whichever one you pick.

The installer is part of the architecture

B-Human’s installer is invasive, and that is a design choice, not a flaw. To be the only one who sees the buttons and the gamepad, it patches two Booster binaries so the original topic names are no longer published. It turns off several Booster services, including the vendor’s camera service, and installs its own camera streaming service on the head board. It changes the password and network settings.

The consequence: once installed, anything that listens on Booster’s original button or gamepad topics, like SDK samples or a ROS 2 soccer stack, gets nothing. There is an uninstall option that restores the patched files, but not every change is undone.

So in practice, you can’t casually run both stacks on one robot. B-Human’s release is tested on Booster firmware 1.7.1 and says 1.8.0 does not behave as intended. My HTWK-route robot runs a 1.8 firmware. Switching one robot between stacks means uninstalling, maybe changing firmware, and checking what is left behind. Where possible, I give each stack its own robot.

Walking policies

The walking inputs show two very different bets:

  • HTWK ParameterWalk: 54 inputs to 12 outputs. Compact, current state plus commands.
  • B-Human walk: 344 inputs on the K1, with a history of 10 steps (200 ms), 12 leg outputs, and an extra output that adjusts the gait frequency. B-Human credits the history and the learned frequency for straighter legs.

I don’t know yet which matters more on our robots. But it is a concrete thing to try in HTWK Gym: add history, let the policy pick its frequency, and compare.

Kicking

Another clear difference:

  • B-Human has two RL kick policies, and the kick policy also does the final approach to the ball. Its inputs include ball velocity, kick direction and strength, and the previous ball position.
  • HTWK Gym has a kicking task with 44 inputs, built around a robot that is already standing in a tight window behind the ball.

Handing the last steps to the kick policy is a big design choice. It means “walk to the ball” and “kick” are not two separate skills with a handover in between. If kicking becomes a priority for us, B-Human’s input design is the reference I’d start from.

Small details that bite

  • Frames. B-Human’s torso frame origin is between the hip pitch joints. Booster’s is 77 mm higher. If you compare or exchange any pose data between the stacks, convert first.
  • Build machine. B-Human’s Linux docs target Ubuntu 26.04 with recent clang, CMake and Qt. My workstation runs 22.04. Instead of upgrading it, I built in a Docker image and cross-compiled for the robot there. SimRobot, their simulator and debugging tool, also runs in a container and connects to the robot remotely.
  • Build type. B-Human’s Develop build is the useful middle: fast enough on the robot, and it can still connect to SimRobot. Release can’t connect. Debug is too slow on the real robot.
  • Licenses. B-Human’s code is released publicly every year. The HTWK Gym snapshot I looked at had no license file, and its README limits competition use of pretrained models to cases agreed with HTWK. Ask before reusing.

So which one?

For now, both, on separate robots.

The HTWK route fits a team that already has a ROS 2 soccer stack and wants to add learned locomotion without replacing everything. Its cost is the handover between firmware and policy, which you have to design and test very carefully.

The B-Human route is a complete, consistent system with years of competition behind it. Its cost is that it takes over the robot, and you accept its architecture, its firmware version and its tools.

Reading both side by side has been the best robotics education I’ve had this year. Each one makes the other’s assumptions visible.

What I took away

  • Compare ownership models, not features. Who owns the joints, the buttons and the safe state tells you more than any feature list.
  • An installer can be architecture. What it disables and patches is part of the design.
  • One robot per stack. Firmware versions and patched binaries make sharing expensive.
  • Read the inputs. The input vector of a policy tells you what its authors believed mattered.
  • Open source in RoboCup is a gift. Both teams published years of work. The least I can do is read it carefully before I change it.

item.title: Exactly One Motion Owner: Running an RL Policy Next to Vendor Firmware
item.description:
A Booster K1 comes with firmware that can already stand, walk, get up and kick. It is a complete product. For RoboCup we wanted to try our own walking: a reinforcement learning policy, trained in simulation, running on the robot and sending joint targets.

The tempting plan is: train the policy, export it, run it, publish joint commands. Done.

The real problem turned out to be something else. Not “how do I run a policy”, but who is moving the legs right now? The firmware can move them. The policy can move them. The soccer behavior sends walk requests. If two of these think they are in charge at the same time, the robot falls.

So the rule we designed around is simple to say: at any moment, exactly one thing owns the motion. This post is what that rule means in practice.

The modes you have to respect

The K1 manual describes a small set of modes:

  • DAMP: joints resist motion but do not hold a posture. Safe for the motors. Not safe for a standing robot, it will fold.
  • PREP: standing posture, but no active balance.
  • WALK: the firmware’s own walking and predefined actions.
  • CUSTOM: developer control. Low-level joint commands from the SDK only take effect here.
  • PROTECT: entered automatically after errors like a fall.

And the transitions are restricted. CUSTOM can only be entered from PREP or DAMP, and can only go back to PREP or DAMP.

So an RL policy lives in CUSTOM. The firmware’s walking lives in WALK. You cannot jump between them directly. Every switch is a handover, and handovers are where robots fall.

Don’t change the soccer code, put a proxy in front

The soccer behavior (a ROS 2 “brain” node with a behavior tree) already sends locomotion requests to the firmware: “walk with this velocity”, “move the head”, “kick”, “get up”. We did not want to fork it.

ROS 2 topic remapping gave us a clean option. At launch, the brain’s request topic is remapped to a bridge. The bridge decides where each request goes:

brain (behavior tree)
   |  locomotion requests (remapped)
   v
bridge
   Firmware owns:  forward request to the firmware
   RL owns:        walk velocity  -> policy input
                   head request   -> head joint targets
                   joint targets  -> single low-level publisher

The brain does not need to know which one is walking. It keeps sending “walk forward at this speed”. The bridge turns that into either a firmware request or a policy command.

One catch: if anyone starts the brain the old way, without the remap, it talks to the firmware directly and bypasses the bridge. So the bridge checks for other publishers on the firmware request topic and on the joint command topic before it takes over. A second writer is a fault, not a warning.

Handing over: firmware to RL

This is the part with the most steps, and each step exists because something can go wrong there:

  1. Warm up the policy first. Run inference on live robot state for a short time while the firmware is still in charge. If inference can’t keep up now, it won’t keep up later.
  2. Ask the firmware to stand still. Zero velocity.
  3. Preload a hold command with the current joint positions. When control switches, the first command the motors see is “stay where you are”, not some default pose.
  4. Create the one and only joint publisher, and confirm nobody else is publishing.
  5. Warm up again under load, now with the high-rate publishing running. If a deadline is missed here, abort and stay with the firmware.
  6. Request CUSTOM once and wait for confirmation. Don’t spam the mode request.
  7. Check that the robot state is fresh.
  8. Ramp in over a couple of seconds from the hold pose to the policy’s output.
  9. Only now accept walk commands from the brain.

The policy runs at 50 Hz. Joint commands go out at 500 Hz. Targets are slew-limited, and a velocity command that is not refreshed in time is set back to zero.

Handing back: RL to firmware

The reverse is shorter, and the order matters:

  1. Mask the brain’s velocity.
  2. Hold a zero command for a moment so the robot settles.
  3. Switch to PREP and confirm the switch.
  4. Remove the joint publisher.

Stopping the publisher and confirming the mode are two different things. If you only stop publishing, the motors keep the last command and you don’t know who is in charge. If you confirm the mode first, you know.

Firmware skills like get-up go through this path too. The bridge first gives control back, confirms it, and only then forwards the skill request. After a firmware skill, the policy does not take over again automatically. Somebody has to enable it again on purpose.

When things go wrong: damping

The fault path is one direction only: request DAMP, then remove the publisher. Faults include:

  • robot state is stale,
  • unsafe posture or a fall,
  • motor error or over-temperature,
  • a second writer appears,
  • the firmware leaves CUSTOM on its own (someone pressed the emergency button),
  • inference misses its deadline.

Damping protects the motors. But remember the first section: a standing robot in damping folds to the ground. So “fault means damping” is the right rule for the hardware, and it is also why a person must be ready to catch or support the robot during these tests. There is no software-only safe stop for a standing humanoid.

The rules I would not relax

Some numbers in this design are tempting to loosen when a check fails: the publish rate, the inference deadline, the maximum age of robot state. Each of those exists because something real depends on it. If a check fails, the check found a problem. Loosening the threshold to make it pass only hides it.

I wrote this down as a rule in the runbook, because on a long test day it is very easy to forget.

What is still open

The bridge knows who owns the motion. The behavior tree does not. It sends a kick request and doesn’t know that the bridge must first hand back to the firmware, or that RL will not resume afterwards. A clean interface that tells the behavior tree “firmware, RL, kick, get-up, fault” is the next piece, and it is still design work.

What I took away

  • Ownership is the real interface. Running the policy was a small part. Deciding and proving who owns the joints was most of the work.
  • One writer, always checked. Never assume you are the only publisher. Check, and treat a second one as a fault.
  • Confirm, don’t assume. A mode request is not a mode change until the robot says so.
  • Put a proxy in front instead of forking. Topic remapping let us change routing without touching the soccer code.
  • Damping is safe for motors, not for people or robots standing up. Plan the physical side of a fault, not only the software side.

item.title: The Robot Saw the Ball and Didn't Move
item.description:
Last week we had a Booster K1 on the field, running the full soccer behavior tree. The robot turned its head and followed the ball. Vision was clearly working. And the robot stood there. It did not walk to the ball.

It took two days to understand. The direct cause was one condition. But on the way there we found four other problems that looked like the same problem. This post is about separating them.

The symptoms, all at once

When we started, everything was mixed together:

  • At first, the vision and brain nodes sometimes failed to start or crashed.
  • With a simple “chase” tree, the robot turned its head but didn’t move its body.
  • With the full game tree, the status log showed the control state set, but the game state empty.
  • At one point the camera RGB topic had no publisher at all.
  • Our nodes and the vendor’s nodes sometimes could not see each other on the ROS 2 network.

It is very tempting to look for one root cause that explains all of this. There wasn’t one. These were different layers failing in different ways, and some of them at the same time.

The direct cause: two conditions, not one

The soccer behavior tree we run has two separate pieces of state:

  • control state: is the robot under autonomous control?
  • game state: what does the referee say? INITIAL, READY, SET, PLAY, END.

When the game tree starts, it sets the control state to “autonomous”. That part was fine. But the normal striker and goalkeeper behavior also requires the game state to be PLAY. And nobody had told the robot the game was playing.

So the robot did everything a robot should do before kick-off. It looked for the ball. It tracked it with its head. It did not walk, because the game had not started. From the outside, that looks exactly like a bug in the chase logic.

The brain also listens to a simple external control topic with string commands: locate, ready, play, stop. Each one sets both pieces of state together. Sending play sets the control state and the game state to PLAY (and also marks the kick-off as ours).

After a restart, we started the game tree and sent play. In the log, the brain received the command, the state changed to PLAY, and about two seconds later the first non-zero turn command appeared. A few seconds after that, the first forward walk command. The robot found the ball and went for it.

Nothing in the chase algorithm or the speed parameters had changed. Only the game state.

Head tracking is not proof of play

This is the lesson I most want to keep. A robot tracking the ball with its head tells you:

  • the camera works,
  • vision detects the ball,
  • the brain receives detections.

It does not tell you that the play behavior is running. Head tracking can happen before PLAY. A correct control mode can happen before PLAY. Both are necessary, neither is sufficient.

Also, a manual play is a test tool. It is not the referee. In a real game, the GameController sends the game state. Getting the robot to move with a manual command proves the behavior works. It does not prove the referee path works. That has to be tested separately.

The other four problems

While chasing the main issue we found and noted the others. I keep them separate because each has a different fix and a different level of “solved”.

The camera. The RGB topic had no publisher. On the firmware version we had, the head camera has to be switched into the right mode through a vendor service call. After that, RGB and detections both came back at a steady rate. This is specific to that firmware. After a firmware update, I check the vendor docs again before assuming the same call works.

The vendor stack. A restart brought back the motion, camera, vision and agent services. A restart is a good cleanup. It is not a fix. If it happens again, we need to know why.

DDS discovery. The Fast DDS profile listed network addresses that were not the ones actually active on the robot that day. That is a good explanation for nodes sometimes not discovering each other. But it is an explanation, not a proven root cause, and it is still open. When nodes are “missing”, I now check three things separately: is the process alive, is the ROS participant discovered, and do messages actually flow.

Startup robustness. We added some hardening: the start script checks that the behavior tree file is installed before stopping the old processes; the launch file checks the tree file name, that it exists, and that the XML parses; the vision node finds its model in the installed package and keeps the error instead of crashing with a null pointer if the model fails to load. None of this was the cause of the “doesn’t move” problem. All of it made the next test less confusing.

A field order I now follow

From this I wrote a short field debug guide. The order is the important part. Each step only makes sense if the step before it is green:

  1. Record versions. Firmware version file and code commit. Without this, any result is hard to compare later.
  2. Vendor services. Are the motion, camera, vision and agent processes actually running? List nodes with --no-daemon, so you don’t read a stale cache.
  3. Camera. Does the RGB topic have a publisher? What is the rate?
  4. Vision. Are detections published, and at what rate?
  5. Brain. Is it running the tree you think it is?
  6. Game state. Is it PLAY? Who set it?
  7. Velocity output. Are non-zero commands coming out?
  8. Motion. Only now look at whether the robot moves.

It is very easy to stare at step 8 and guess about steps 2 to 7. That is where the time goes.

What I’d like to have next time

  • A low-frequency, structured log of brain state changes. Finding “received play” among thousands of debug lines is slow.
  • A regression list I actually run: robot stays still with no game state; starts after PLAY; returns to zero after STOP; manual path and referee path tested separately; one change at a time.

What I took away

  • Many symptoms, many causes. Don’t force one story onto five problems.
  • Know every gate on the path to motion. Control mode and game state were two gates, and I only knew about one.
  • Head tracking proves perception, not behavior.
  • A restart is cleanup, not a fix. Write down what it cleaned up.
  • Debug from the bottom up. Services, camera, vision, brain, game state, velocity, then motion. In that order.

item.title: Hearing the Referee: Whistle Detection on an ARM Robot
item.description:
In RoboCup humanoid soccer, the referee uses a whistle. For some game state changes, like kick-off going from “set” to “playing”, robots are expected to hear the whistle themselves. The official GameController sends the same “playing” signal too, but with a delay. A robot that hears the whistle can start moving earlier.

So our robot needed ears. The pipeline is simple to describe:

microphone (ALSA)
  -> AlsaWhistleDetector
  -> TFLiteWhistleDetection (features + small neural net)
  -> whistle_detector_node publishes /whistle_detection/detected
  -> brain node subscribes
  -> behavior / game state

Making it actually work on the robot took much longer than writing that diagram. Almost none of the problems were about the neural network.

Problem 1: the library was the wrong CPU

The detector code came with TensorFlow Lite bundled as static libraries. For x86_64. Our workstations are x86_64. The robot is aarch64.

So it built and ran on my laptop, and the robot build failed at CMake configure. On the robot there was no system TensorFlow Lite either. Nothing under /usr or /usr/local.

The fix was to build the TensorFlow Lite C API for ARM64 myself, as a shared library, and keep it inside the repository:

  1. On an Ubuntu x86_64 machine, install the AArch64 cross toolchain and Bazelisk.
  2. Clone TensorFlow and pin a release branch.
  3. Run ./configure with CUDA, ROCm, Android and iOS all off.
  4. Build only the C library:
bazel build --config=elinux_aarch64 -c opt \
  //tensorflow/lite/c:libtensorflowlite_c.so
  1. Check that what you built is really what you think:
file libtensorflowlite_c.so
readelf -h libtensorflowlite_c.so | grep Machine   # AArch64
readelf -d libtensorflowlite_c.so | grep NEEDED    # only libc, libm, libstdc++...
  1. Copy the .so and the C headers into the package’s 3rdparty folder under an aarch64 directory.

Then CMake picks the backend by architecture. There was one more trap. The build had a stub fallback: if no TensorFlow Lite was found, it built a detector that compiles, runs, and never detects anything. Good for keeping the build green. Terrible on a robot, because everything looks fine.

So on the robot we build with the stub explicitly disabled:

colcon build --packages-select whistle_detector --symlink-install \
  --cmake-args -DWHISTLE_DETECTOR_ALLOW_STUB_FALLBACK=OFF

and look for one line in the output: using repo TensorFlow Lite library: .../aarch64/libtensorflowlite_c.so. If it says “disabled stub”, stop.

Problem 2: two Python environments

To build TensorFlow I created a Python virtual environment. Later I ran colcon build for the ROS workspace from the same shell. ROS message generation failed with:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'em'

colcon had picked the virtualenv’s python3, which did not have ROS’s Python dependencies. Nothing wrong with the code. Wrong shell.

The rule now: the TensorFlow build shell is only for TensorFlow. ROS builds happen in a clean ROS shell.

Problem 3: who starts the detector?

At first the detector was started by the brain’s launch file, as a child. The start script did not make that clear, and the stop script did not stop the detector at all. So you could end up with an old detector still holding the microphone.

We changed it to two independent processes. The brain only subscribes to the topic. It never touches the microphone, and it does not spawn the detector. There is a script to start everything, one to start only the detector, one to start only the brain, and the stop script stops both.

It is a small change, but now “is the detector running?” has one answer, and you can test each side alone.

Problem 4: “the microphone is open” is not “the microphone works”

ALSA can open a device successfully and then deliver no audio. Or deliver audio from the wrong device. On a robot with several audio routes, default is not always what you want.

The detector expects a very specific format: capture, interleaved, S16_LE, 2 channels, 44100 Hz. It does not resample or remap channels. So the first test is outside ROS:

arecord -l
arecord -D default -f S16_LE -c 2 -r 44100 -d 3 /tmp/whistle_test.wav

Then I added logs that separate the states that used to look the same:

  • device opened,
  • device opened but no frames yet,
  • microphone input is active, received N frames,
  • overrun, recovering.

Only the third one counts as “microphone online”. Two other small ALSA fixes came from comparing with a known-good capture example: call snd_pcm_prepare() explicitly before the read loop, and use snd_pcm_drop() instead of snd_pcm_drain() when closing a capture device.

Problem 5: a cooldown that never cooled down

After a detection, the node waits for a cooldown before publishing again. The “last publish” time was initialised to steady_clock::time_point::min().

That looks reasonable: “long, long ago”. But now() - min() overflows a signed 64-bit duration. My reading is that the cooldown check got a garbage value and never let the first detection through. Initialising it to now() - cooldown - 1ms fixed it.

One more small crash in the same area: cooldown_ms was declared as a double parameter, and the launch file passed 1500. ROS 2 is strict about parameter types and threw InvalidParameterTypeException. It had to be 1500.0.

Two logs that tell you everything

The most useful thing I added was two log lines, one on each side of the topic:

  • detector: upstream whistle detector hit: published detection with confidence ...
  • brain: whistleDetectionCallback triggered: whistle detected at ... s

Now the diagnosis is a table:

Detector log Brain log Meaning
no no detector not triggering, not running, or on the stub
yes no detection works, brain is not receiving it
yes yes the chain is connected

grep on two log files answers a question that used to take a lot of guessing.

What tests can and can’t tell you

I added unit tests for the detector: a whistle-like tone should be detected, silence and an off-band tone should be rejected, and reset() should clear the streaming state. They pass.

They test the model and the windowing logic. They do not test the microphone. Synthetic tones are not a referee in a noisy hall. In real testing we saw false positives even with a strict confidence threshold, so threshold tuning with real field recordings is still open work.

And there was a bigger lesson. In a game test, the whistle was detected, but the robot was not in the ready or playing behavior we expected. The ears worked. The state handling around them did not, and we have not fully closed that yet.

That changed how I think about the feature. Hearing correctly is not the hard part. Deciding who is allowed to change the game state is. The GameController is the official source of game state. If the whistle can also change it, you now have two referees inside one robot, and they will sometimes disagree. My plan from here is to keep the GameController as the authority, and treat the whistle as an extra signal that is logged and checked, until we can prove the two never fight.

What I took away

  • The model was the easy part. Cross-compiling, Python environments, process ownership and audio routing took most of the time.
  • Never let a stub pass silently. A fallback that compiles but does nothing must be turned off on the real target.
  • Log the boundaries. One log line on each side of a topic turns debugging into a lookup table.
  • Opened is not working. Only count a sensor as online when real data arrives.
  • Detection is not authority. Before a signal changes the robot’s state, decide who owns that state.

item.title: Week One for Interns: Git, ROS 2 and a Real Humanoid
item.description:
This summer our lab had a group of interns joining the RoboCup humanoid soccer work. The robot is a Booster T1. The software is ROS 2 on Ubuntu.

I prepared the material for the first week. This post is how I planned it and why it is in that order.

The goal of week one

Not “learn robotics”. That takes years.

The goal was smaller: by the end of the week, every intern can change code in a shared robot repository without breaking anything for anybody else. If they can do that, everything after week one is learning. If they can’t, everything after week one is cleaning up.

So the order was:

  1. Git, for real teamwork.
  2. ROS 2 installation and core concepts.
  3. A tour of the actual RoboCup project.
  4. A small hands-on ROS 2 project, done with Git.

The robot itself comes last on purpose.

Git first, not ROS first

It is tempting to start with the exciting part. A humanoid robot is right there in the room.

But on a robot team, the most common way a new person causes damage is not a bad algorithm. It is git add . with build artifacts, a log file and a debug change mixed in. Or a commit directly on main the day before a test.

So the Git session was not a list of commands. It was organised around one mental model and a list of real mistakes.

The mental model is four places: the working directory (what you are editing), the staging area (what goes into the next commit), the local repository (saved history), and the remote (the shared copy on GitHub). Almost every Git confusion is “which of the four places is my change in right now?”

The habit I pushed hardest is git status. Before add, before commit, before pull, before push. It costs nothing and it answers the question above.

Then the common mistakes, one per topic:

  • Committing with messages like update, fix, final.
  • Huge commits that mix unrelated changes.
  • Working directly on main.
  • Switching branches with uncommitted work and getting lost.
  • Pulling with many uncommitted local changes.
  • Force pushing a shared branch without asking.
  • git reset --hard without knowing what it throws away.
  • Keeping important work only in a stash for days.

I find mistakes teach better than rules. “Never commit build artifacts” is easy to agree with and easy to forget. A concrete picture of what goes wrong is harder to forget.

A Git practice repository

Slides are not enough for Git. You need to feel a merge conflict once in a safe place.

So I made a small practice repository. It has a README, a file for intern information, a robot startup checklist, a safety rules file, a small Python script and a .gitignore. Each task asks the intern to change one of them, on their own branch, and open a pull request.

The content of the files is not random. The startup checklist asks things like “verify battery level, check network connection, confirm emergency stop status”. The safety rules file asks for at least three rules in professional language. So while practising Git, they are also writing the first version of habits they will need next to a real robot.

Interns could work alone or in small groups. Either way, the rule was the same: never on main, always a named branch, always a pull request.

ROS 2: four ideas and a few commands

For ROS 2 we used Ubuntu 22.04 and ROS 2 Humble, the same as the robot project. I wrote an installation guide for that exact setup, including the errors students usually hit, like a missing rosidl_default_generators package.

The concepts session was kept to four communication ideas:

  • Topics for continuous data, like camera images and robot state.
  • Services for quick request and response.
  • Actions for long goals with feedback and cancel, like navigation.
  • Parameters for runtime configuration, instead of constants in code.

Each idea came with the command to see it on a running system: ros2 topic list, ros2 topic echo, ros2 service list, ros2 param get. I wanted them to look at a live ROS graph before they write a node.

Then workspaces and packages: src, build, install, log, and the one rule that saves the most time in the first week: source the workspace after you build.

A tour of the real project

After the basics, we walked through the RoboCup software as it actually is. The stack has layers:

RoboCup application
ROS 2 middleware
Booster SDK
Robot OS / drivers
Robot hardware

The key point for new people: application code uses the supported ROS 2 interfaces and SDK APIs. It does not talk to the hardware directly.

The application itself is a few nodes. Vision detects the ball and the field. A game controller node receives the referee’s game state. A whistle detector listens to the referee. A central “brain” node combines all of this, runs the behavior, and sends motion requests down to the SDK.

I also told them where bugs usually live on a robot. Most of them are not in the algorithm. They are sensor, timing, network, configuration or state machine problems. On a distributed robot, the DDS network configuration is part of the runtime, not something you set once and forget.

The hands-on project

The last part tied everything together. Each intern cloned a starter repository, created a branch with their name, and built a ROS 2 Python package with two nodes: a talker that publishes a string on a topic, and a listener that subscribes and prints it.

Then they had to inspect their own system with the CLI tools, commit, push, and open a pull request.

It is the most basic ROS 2 example there is. That is the point. It touches every step of the real workflow once: workspace, package, build, source, run, inspect, commit, push, review. When they later work on the vision or behavior code, the steps are the same. Only the code inside is harder.

What I took away

  • Teach the workflow before the robot. The robot is the reward. The workflow is what keeps the robot running for everybody.
  • Teach mistakes, not commands. Every Git command in the slides came with the way people misuse it.
  • Make practice files useful. A startup checklist and safety rules are better practice content than “hello world” text.
  • Keep the first ROS project tiny. A talker and a listener are enough to walk through the whole pipeline once.
  • Show where real bugs live. New people expect bugs in algorithms. On a robot, they are mostly in timing, networking and configuration.

item.title: A Tour of AVLite, a Simplified AV Stack
item.description:
A full autonomous driving stack is too big to read in one go. Autoware has hundreds of packages. You open it, you read the launch files for a day, and you still don’t know where one loop iteration starts and ends.

AVLite is the opposite. It is a simplified AV stack in Python: perception, localization, planning, control, a simulator bridge and a GUI, small enough to hold in your head. I spent some time reading it with one goal: follow one control step from start to end, and write down the map.

This post is that map.

The layout

The top-level modules are numbered, which I liked immediately:

c10_perception     perception, localization, HD map interfaces
c20_planning       global and local planning
c30_control        controller interface and implementations
c40_execution      runtime wiring, execution loop, world bridges
c50_visualization  GUI
c60_common         settings, reload helpers, capability enums
extensions/        plugin-style extensions

The numbers tell you the order data flows through the system. It is a small thing, but when you open the folder you already see the architecture. I wish more codebases did this.

The entry point starts a Tkinter GUI. So AVLite is GUI-first. You run it and you watch the car, which is exactly what you want when you are learning or trying a new planner.

The most important file

If you want to understand how the system boots, don’t start from main. Start from the factory in c40_execution.

The factory is where everything is assembled. It:

  • loads extensions,
  • picks the strategies named in the config from registries,
  • loads the global plan,
  • creates one shared PerceptionModel,
  • wires planner, controller, world bridge, localization and perception together,
  • returns the selected executor.

After reading this one file, the rest of the code made sense. Before reading it, every module looked like it floated on its own.

How modules are plugged in

AVLite uses subclass auto-registration. You write a subclass of, say, a controller base class, you import it, and it becomes selectable by name in the config.

That is very good for research. Want to compare two lateral controllers? Write the second one, change one string in the config, run again. No wiring code to touch.

The cost is the usual cost of string-based wiring. A typo in the config is only found at runtime. And as the number of plugins grows, “which class is actually running?” becomes a real question. I learned to always check the effective class at startup, not just the default in the config file.

The key abstractions

There are only a handful, and each has one job:

  • GlobalPlan. Loaded from a JSON track file: reference XY path, reference speed profile, left and right boundaries. The static backbone of the drive.
  • PerceptionModel. The shared environment memory: ego vehicle, other vehicles, optional HD map, predictions, occupancy grids. Several modules read from it and write into it.
  • WorldBridge. The interface to the outside world. A simple built-in simulator, or bridges to CARLA or Gazebo. It gives the current ego state, sensor data and ground truth, and it accepts control commands.
  • LocalPlanner. Generates and selects a short-term maneuver.
  • Controller. Takes the ego state and a trajectory, returns a control command.
  • Executor. The loop that calls all of the above in order.

One step of the loop

This is the part I most wanted to understand. In the synchronous executor, one step goes like this:

  1. Read the ego state from the world. world.get_ego_state() is the source of truth for this instant: x, y, heading, speed.
  2. Replan if it is time. A replan_dt setting decides how often. The default local planner is a greedy lattice planner. It samples nodes in Frenet coordinates (distance along the track, and offset from it), builds candidate edges, rejects edges that collide or curve too much, and keeps the best chain as the selected local plan.
  3. Advance the planner with the current pose. The planner updates where the car is on the global and local trajectory. This keeps planner and controller in agreement about “where are we on the plan”.
  4. Run the controller. The default is a Stanley controller. It computes cross-track error and heading error against the local trajectory, reads the target speed from it, and produces steering and speed commands.
  5. Send the command to the world.
  6. Run localization and perception, if enabled. They update the shared model for the next step.

Written as one line:

WorldBridge -> LocalPlanner (replan, step) -> Controller -> WorldBridge
                     ^                                         |
                     +---- PerceptionModel <-- perception -----+

The nice detail is that localization and perception are optional. In a simple simulator you can use ground truth and turn them off, and the rest of the loop does not change. When you want to test a localization algorithm, you turn it on and nothing else has to know.

A debugging checklist that falls out of the map

Once the loop is clear, debugging becomes a question of which transformation failed:

  • Was the world state read correctly?
  • Is the perception model fresh, or stale from an earlier step?
  • Did the planner generate reasonable candidates?
  • Is the planner’s idea of “where am I on the plan” aligned with the real pose?
  • Is the controller tracking the trajectory it was given?
  • Was the command actually applied by the world bridge?

When the car does something strange, I go down this list in order. It is much faster than staring at the GUI.

Rough edges

AVLite is research code and it shows in a few places:

  • The factory does a lot. It is the best place to start reading, and also the file most likely to grow into a god object.
  • Timing deserves attention. Sim time versus control time, and sync versus async execution, are where modular stacks usually start to break.
  • Naming is a bit rough here and there (Executer, ControlComand). Not a real problem, but it tells you nobody has done a cleanup pass yet.

None of this stops it from being useful. For learning and quick experiments, a stack you can fully read beats a stack you can only configure.

What I took away

  • Find the assembly point first. In AVLite it is the factory. In an Android app it was Application.onCreate(). Same idea: read where things are wired before reading what they do.
  • One loop iteration is the real architecture. Folder structure tells you the intent. The loop tells you the truth.
  • Small stacks teach big ones. Every abstraction here, the world bridge, the shared model, the planner/controller split, exists in the large stacks too. They are just easier to see when there are six of them instead of six hundred.
  • Real modularity versus apparent modularity. Registries make everything look pluggable. The question to ask is whether timing and capability assumptions still hold when you swap something in.

item.title: Four Questions an Android Engineer Asked When Switching to Autonomous Vehicles
item.description:
I wrote C++ for a few years, then Android for about seven, then more mobile work in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. At the end of 2025 I moved to a research job at a university lab in Abu Dhabi. One of the projects is autonomous racing.

The first weeks felt strange. I could read the code. I could build it. But I did not really understand why the stack was split the way it was. Words like “path”, “trajectory”, “pose” and “frame” were used all the time, and everybody seemed to agree on what they meant except me.

So I did what I used to do with Android source: I wrote down the questions that kept blocking me, and I worked through them one by one until the answer was short enough to remember. There were four.

1. Does planning output a path or a trajectory?

I used both words as if they were the same. They are not.

  • A path is geometry. A curve in space, x(s), y(s), parameterized by distance along the curve. It answers: where should I go?
  • A trajectory is a path with time. x(t), y(t), heading(t), v(t), a(t). It answers: where should I be at each moment, and how fast?

The rule of thumb I now use: does the output include time, or velocity? If no, it is a path. If yes, it is a trajectory.

Why does it matter? Because a controller needs time. It computes an error between where the car is and where it should be now. With only a path, “now” is not defined. The controller does not know how fast to go or when to brake.

In a typical stack, the global planner gives a path (a route along the map, no timing). The local or motion planner turns that into a trajectory, with speed and acceleration limits and obstacles. The controller tracks the trajectory.

Small mobile robots often hide this. In ROS Nav2, for example, the global planner outputs a path and the local planner computes velocity commands on the fly. The path-to-trajectory step is still there. It is just inside one module.

At racing speed you cannot hide it. You cannot decide speed only at the last moment in the controller. Speed has to be planned together with the curve.

The Android comparison that helped me: a path is the shape of an animation, a trajectory is the shape plus the interpolator and the duration. Without the time part, nothing moves.

2. Where is the boundary between perception and localization?

Both use the same sensors: camera, LiDAR, IMU, GNSS. Sometimes even the same features. So where is the line?

The answer that finally worked for me is: what is the subject of the estimate?

  • Perception estimates the state of the world: other cars, their positions and speeds, lanes, free space.
  • Localization estimates the state of me: my position, heading and velocity in the map.

Or in transform language: if a module estimates T_map_base, it is localization. If it estimates T_base_object, it is perception.

Perception says “there is a car 12 meters ahead”. Localization says “I am at this point in the map”. Without localization, the perception output is floating. It is relative to a car whose position nobody knows.

Some things sit on the line. SLAM builds a map (perception of structure) and estimates the pose (localization) at the same time. Lane detection is perception, but matching those lanes to an HD map to correct your pose is localization. Same raw data, different question.

For me this was the same lesson as layering an app: don’t split modules by what data they read, split them by what they are responsible for producing.

3. Why is the TF tree so important?

In Android, coordinates were mostly a UI problem. A view has its own coordinates, the parent has others, the screen has others. You convert, and if you get it wrong a button is drawn a few pixels off.

In a car the same mistake moves an obstacle by a meter.

Every module lives in some frame. A typical tree looks like this:

map
 └── odom
      └── base_link
           ├── lidar
           ├── camera_front
           └── imu

The LiDAR sees a car at (8.2, 1.1) in the LiDAR frame. The planner needs it in the map frame. So you chain the transforms: map to base (from localization), base to LiDAR (from calibration), LiDAR to object (from perception). If any link is wrong, objects shift, lanes don’t line up, and the planner plans around things that are not there.

The part I underestimated was time. Transforms change every moment, so you need the transform at the timestamp of the measurement. A small delay is harmless when you are slow. At 1 m/s, a 100 ms error is 10 cm. At 30 m/s, the same 100 ms is 3 meters.

People say most “mysterious” bugs in robotics are TF bugs. After a few weeks I started to believe them.

4. What does a vehicle controller actually take as input?

I expected a long list. In the end it is three things:

  1. Where I should be. The reference trajectory from the planner: positions, headings, speeds, sometimes acceleration, with timestamps.
  2. Where I am. The state estimate: pose, velocity, yaw rate, steering angle.
  3. What I am allowed to do. Vehicle parameters (wheelbase, max steering angle, max acceleration) and limits (steering rate, jerk, speed caps).

Plus some mode information, like whether we are in emergency braking.

What the controller does not take is just as useful to know: no camera images, no point clouds, no list of detected objects. All of that is already turned into a trajectory upstream. The controller lives in a much simpler world. It assumes the trajectory it gets is safe and feasible.

Controllers are also often split in two:

  • Lateral (steering) needs curvature, heading error, cross-track error, and current speed. Speed matters because the same steering angle does very different things at 20 km/h and at 200 km/h.
  • Longitudinal (throttle and brake) needs the reference speed and acceleration and the current speed.

This split is clean on paper. In racing it is not, because tires have a limited amount of grip, and braking and turning both use it. But that is a topic for another post.

What I took away

  • Ask “what does it output?” before “how does it work?” Every one of these four questions became easy once I looked at a module’s output, not its algorithm.
  • Time is part of the data. Paths without time and transforms without timestamps both look fine until the car moves fast.
  • Old habits still work. Reading Android source taught me to draw the data flow first. It is the same here, only the data is in meters instead of pixels.
  • Write the questions down. They felt too basic to ask out loud. Written down, they had short answers, and those answers became the map I still use.

item.title: Flutter's Three Trees, for People Who Wrote Android Views
item.description:
In the last post I mapped Flutter words to Android words. One row in that table was wrong in a useful way: “setState() is like invalidate()”. It is not. To see why, you need Flutter’s three trees.

On Android there is one tree. A View is the configuration, the state and the thing that measures and draws, all in one object. You call requestLayout() when the size may change and invalidate() when the pixels change. I wrote custom Views for years with this model in my head.

Flutter splits that one object into three.

Three trees, three jobs

Widget. An immutable description. Padding(padding: 8, child: ...) is just data. It is created on every build and thrown away. Creating one is very cheap.

Element. The live instance at one position in the tree. It holds a reference to the current widget, to its parent and children, and, for a StatefulWidget, the State object. The BuildContext you get in build() is the Element. This is the part that lives long.

RenderObject. The part that does layout, paint and hit testing. If you know onMeasure(), onLayout() and onDraw(), this is where they live: performLayout() and paint().

My notes first said “every widget has one Element and one RenderObject”. That is not quite right, and the difference matters:

  • Every widget creates one Element.
  • Only RenderObjectWidgets create a RenderObject. Padding, Align, RichText, CustomPaint are examples.
  • StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget only compose other widgets. Their Elements have no RenderObject of their own.

For example, Text is a StatelessWidget. Its build() returns a RichText, and the RichText creates a RenderParagraph. So the render tree is much smaller than the widget tree. Most of the widgets you write are just glue.

What happens on setState

Say a counter changes from 1 to 2.

  1. setState() runs your callback and calls markNeedsBuild() on this Element. The Element is added to a dirty list, and a frame is scheduled. Nothing else happens yet.
  2. On the next frame, Flutter calls build() on each dirty Element. Your build() returns a new Text('2').
  3. For each child, Flutter compares the old widget with the new one. If they can be matched (rules below), the old Element is kept and gets the new widget through update().
  4. Down the tree, RichText calls updateRenderObject(). It sets the new text on the existing RenderParagraph.
  5. The RenderObject’s setter checks if the value really changed. If yes, it calls markNeedsLayout() or markNeedsPaint().
  6. Later in the same frame, only the marked RenderObjects run layout and paint.

So setState() is not invalidate(). markNeedsPaint() is the real invalidate(), and markNeedsLayout() is the real requestLayout(). Rebuild is an extra step that Android Views do not have. The closest Android thing is recomposition in Jetpack Compose.

Element reuse

Step 3 is where performance and state are decided. The rule is in Widget.canUpdate(): an old Element can take a new widget if the two widgets have the same runtime type and the same key. That’s all.

Children without keys are matched by position. Children with keys are matched by key. If the parent Element is replaced, all its children are replaced too.

Two cases taught me why this matters.

Changing the type at a position loses state.

// before
child: MyForm()
// after, a condition wraps it
child: isWide ? Padding(padding: p, child: MyForm()) : MyForm()

When isWide flips, the widget at that position changes from MyForm to Padding. Different type, so the old Element is thrown away, and with it the State of MyForm. Whatever the user typed is gone. The fix is to keep the tree shape stable, for example always wrap with Padding and change only the padding value.

Reordering without keys moves the wrong thing.

My notes said that if you swap two Text widgets without keys, both are destroyed and rebuilt. That is not what happens. The types match at each position, so both Elements are reused. Each one just gets the other widget’s config. For Text this is fine, the screen looks correct.

The real problem is with stateful children. Say a list of two items, each with a checkbox state inside its own State. The user checks the first one, then you swap the items. The Elements stay in place, and so do their State objects. The labels move, but the checked state does not. Now the wrong item looks checked.

children: items.map((item) => TodoTile(
  key: ValueKey(item.id),
  item: item,
)).toList(),

With a ValueKey, Flutter matches by key. The Element, and its State, moves together with the item. This is the same idea as giving stable IDs to RecyclerView items, so the adapter knows which row is which.

A GlobalKey goes one step further. It lets an Element keep its state even when it moves to a different parent. It is also more expensive, so I only use it when I really need that, or to reach a State from outside, like a FormState.

Rebuild is not repaint

Once the three trees are clear, this follows:

  • Rebuild happens in the Widget and Element trees. build() runs, new widgets are compared with old ones.
  • Repaint happens in the RenderObject tree. paint() runs and records drawing commands into a layer.

They are independent. A rebuild where nothing really changed ends at step 5 above: the setters see the same values and do not mark anything. No layout, no paint.

And a repaint can happen without any rebuild. A CustomPainter can take a repaint: listenable, like an AnimationController. When the animation ticks, only paint() runs again. No build(), no diff. For a smooth animation this is the cheapest path.

One note I had to correct: “rebuild costs CPU, repaint costs GPU”. It is not that clean. Build, layout and paint all run on the UI thread, on the CPU. Paint only records commands. The GPU work happens later, when the raster thread turns the layers into pixels. Both rebuild and repaint cost CPU time on the UI thread, and that is the budget you have to stay inside, about 16ms per frame at 60Hz.

RepaintBoundary

By default a RenderObject paints into the same layer as its parent. If the parent repaints, the children repaint too.

RepaintBoundary gives a subtree its own layer. If something next to it repaints, the boundary’s layer can be reused as is. If something inside it repaints, the work stays inside the boundary. A spinning loader next to a complex chart is a good case: put each in its own boundary and the chart is not repainted 60 times a second.

It is not free. Every layer costs memory and compositing time. To check if it helps, turn on debugRepaintRainbowEnabled. Each repainted area changes color, so you can see what repaints when it should not.

When to write your own RenderObject

On Android, when the standard layouts were not enough, I wrote a custom ViewGroup. In Flutter the equivalent is a custom RenderObject. But it is lower level than a custom View, and usually you don’t need it. I try these first, in order:

  1. Compose existing widgets.
  2. CustomPaint for custom drawing.
  3. CustomMultiChildLayout or Flow for custom positioning.

A custom RenderObject makes sense for a layout the standard ones can’t express, like a real waterfall layout, or for a custom hit test, like a round or polygon-shaped button. The pattern has two parts: a widget that creates and updates the RenderObject, and the RenderObject itself. The part that is easy to get wrong is the setter:

class RenderBar extends RenderBox {
  RenderBar(this._factor);

  double _factor;
  set factor(double value) {
    if (value == _factor) return;
    _factor = value;
    markNeedsLayout(); // size depends on it
  }

  @override
  void performLayout() {
    size = constraints.constrain(Size(100 * _factor, 50));
  }

  @override
  void paint(PaintingContext context, Offset offset) {
    context.canvas.drawRect(offset & size, Paint()..color = const Color(0xFF2196F3));
  }
}

class Bar extends LeafRenderObjectWidget {
  const Bar({super.key, required this.factor});
  final double factor;

  @override
  RenderBar createRenderObject(BuildContext context) => RenderBar(factor);

  @override
  void updateRenderObject(BuildContext context, RenderBar renderObject) {
    renderObject.factor = factor;
  }
}

If the setter just assigns the field and forgets markNeedsLayout(), the new value is stored but nothing on screen changes. If it always marks, even for the same value, you lose the “rebuild without repaint” benefit. The early return is what makes rebuilds cheap.

What I took away

  • Android’s one View is Flutter’s three objects. Widget is the config, Element is the instance with state, RenderObject is the measure-layout-draw part.
  • markNeedsPaint() is invalidate(). setState() is not. Rebuild is a separate, earlier step.
  • Type and key decide if state survives. Keep the tree shape stable, and give list items keys.
  • Rebuild is not repaint. Many rebuilds are cheap because nothing below them changes. Most real cost is in what you do inside build().
  • Custom RenderObjects are the last tool, not the first. Composition and CustomPaint cover most cases.

item.title: Flutter for Android Engineers
item.description:
I wrote Android apps for about seven years. When I started learning Flutter this year, the hardest part was not Dart. Dart is easy if you know Java and Kotlin. The hard part was that every Flutter word looked like an Android word I already knew, and the match was almost right, but not quite.

So I made a table. Every time I met a new concept, I wrote down the Android thing it reminded me of, and then where the comparison breaks. This post is that table, cleaned up.

The short version

Flutter Closest Android thing Where it breaks
Widget View / ViewGroup A widget is cheap, immutable config. It is not the thing on screen.
StatefulWidget + State A View plus the fields that drive it The State object lives longer than the widget.
setState() change a field + invalidate() It schedules a rebuild for the next frame. It does not draw.
BuildContext Context It is a position in the tree, not an app-wide handle.
Navigator.push / pop startActivity / finish Routes are not Activities. One Activity hosts them all.
InheritedWidget / Provider ViewModel + LiveData Scoped to a subtree, not global.
Future / async / await coroutines No Dispatchers.IO. One thread per isolate.
Stream Flow / LiveData Close enough.
AnimationController / Tween ValueAnimator / TypeEvaluator Close enough.
Hot reload Apply Changes Much faster, and it keeps state.

Now the details.

Widget is not View

On Android a View is a real object that stays on screen. You hold a reference to it and change it: textView.setText("Hello").

In Flutter you never do that. A Text("Hello") is just a description. It is immutable and very cheap. When the data changes, you build a new Text("World") and Flutter works out what to change on screen. You describe the UI as a function of state, and you stop thinking about references.

If you have used Jetpack Compose, this part is familiar. If you only wrote XML layouts and findViewById, this is the biggest mental change. It took me a few days before I stopped looking for “the reference to the text view”.

StatelessWidget is for things that only depend on their constructor arguments. StatefulWidget is for things that have their own changing data.

State, and why build lives there

A StatefulWidget comes with a separate State class, and build() is on the State, not on the widget. This looked strange to me at first.

The reason is lifetime. The widget is thrown away and rebuilt all the time. The State object stays, as long as the widget keeps its place in the tree. So the data that must survive, like a counter or a scroll position, lives in State, and build() reads from it.

class _CounterState extends State<Counter> {
  int _count = 0;

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return TextButton(
      onPressed: () => setState(() => _count++),
      child: Text('$_count'),
    );
  }
}

setState() is like “change the field and call invalidate()”, but there is a difference. It only marks this part of the tree as dirty. On the next frame Flutter calls build() again and compares the result with the old one. Nothing is drawn inside setState() itself.

One Android habit that transfers directly: after an async call, check that you are still alive before touching the UI. On Android I used to check isAdded() on a Fragment, or the lifecycle state. In Flutter it is if (!mounted) return; before calling setState().

The lifecycle methods also map roughly:

  • initState() is like onCreate(), but for this widget, not the whole screen.
  • dispose() is like onDestroy(). Cancel controllers and subscriptions here.
  • For the app going to background, there is WidgetsBindingObserver or AppLifecycleListener, which feel like onPause() and onResume().

BuildContext is not Context

This one confused me the most, because the name is so similar.

An Android Context is a handle to the app and the system. You use it to get resources, start Activities, get system services. Any Context from your app can do roughly the same things.

A BuildContext is the location of a widget in the tree. Under the hood it is the Element object (more on Elements in the next post). When you call Theme.of(context) or Navigator.of(context), Flutter walks up the tree from that location and finds the nearest one.

So which context you use matters. A classic mistake: in the same build() method that creates a Scaffold, you call Scaffold.of(context). It fails, because that context is above the Scaffold, not inside it. The fix is to use a Builder, or move the code into a child widget, so you get a context below it.

The other rule: don’t keep a BuildContext after an await without checking context.mounted. The widget may be gone. This is the same kind of bug as holding an Activity Context too long on Android, just with a different symptom.

Navigation

Navigator.push() and pop() work like a back stack. pushReplacement() is like startActivity() followed by finish(). Named routes feel like starting a screen with an Intent action or a deep link.

The difference: these routes are not Activities. A Flutter app usually runs inside one FlutterActivity, and all the screens are drawn by Flutter inside it. There is no system back stack per screen, no launchMode, and no process death per screen to think about. I found this simpler.

Sharing state

My notes first said “InheritedWidget is like a singleton”. That is not right. An InheritedWidget gives data to its subtree. Two different subtrees can have two different values. Widgets below that read it with context.dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType() are rebuilt when it changes.

A better match: Provider or Riverpod on top of a ChangeNotifier feels like ViewModel plus LiveData. You expose state, the UI listens, the UI rebuilds. The scoping is by tree position instead of by Activity or Fragment.

Async: the part that really breaks

Future with async / await reads almost like a Kotlin suspend function. Stream is close to Flow, and StreamBuilder feels like observing LiveData in a Fragment.

But the threading model is different, and this is the one place where my Android instinct was wrong.

On Android, I would write withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } and the work runs on another thread. In Dart, each isolate has one thread with an event loop. await http.get(...) does not block the UI, because the network IO itself is asynchronous and the result comes back as an event. But if you parse a huge JSON or resize an image in Dart code, that runs on the UI isolate and you will drop frames. There is no IO dispatcher to switch to.

For heavy CPU work you start another isolate, for example with Isolate.run() or compute(). Isolates do not share memory. You send data in and get data back. It feels closer to a separate process than a thread.

Animation and tools

AnimationController is like ValueAnimator: it produces values over time. A Tween maps 0..1 to the values you want, like a TypeEvaluator. The vsync argument ties the controller to the screen refresh, similar to what Choreographer does on Android.

Hot reload deserves a line. It injects the new code and rebuilds the widgets while keeping the State. After years of waiting for Gradle, this changed how I worked. I tried small UI changes much more often because it cost a second.

What I took away

  • Map the new words to the old ones, but write down where the map breaks. The breaks are where the bugs are.
  • Widgets are descriptions, not objects on screen. Once this clicked, most of Flutter made sense.
  • BuildContext is a position. Most of my early errors were using the context from the wrong place.
  • Watch the threading. async is not “off the main thread”. Heavy work still needs an isolate.

The row “rebuild vs invalidate” in the table is the most misleading one. Flutter actually keeps three trees, and a rebuild is not a redraw. That is the next post.

item.title: Spring Boot from the Other Side of the API
item.description:
Two years ago I wrote a quick tour of Spring Boot. It was about the surface: starters, YAML config, REST style, how easy it is to add a library. This spring I went back to Java backend, this time slower and with a plan.

I am an Android engineer. For years I have been on the client side of the API: calling endpoints, parsing JSON, retrying when the network is bad. This time I wanted to understand the other side. This post is about what I could reuse from Android, and what I had to learn from zero.

The plan

I wrote a seven-day plan to get the whole map first and the details later:

  1. Java basics from a backend view: collections, thread pools, Java 8 streams and Optional. Plus HTTP itself.
  2. Spring Boot and IoC/DI.
  3. Spring MVC and a small REST API.
  4. Persistence: JDBC, JPA, MyBatis.
  5. AOP, transactions, Spring Security basics.
  6. Redis, message queues, the basic ideas of distributed systems.
  7. Build and deploy: Maven, a runnable jar, Docker, logs.

Seven days was too short, of course. The plan gave me the order. Then I spent the next weeks going through a Spring Boot course and taking notes: auto-configuration, bean scanning, a custom starter, JWT, ThreadLocal, testing, the data layer, caching.

The rule I set for myself was simple: for every new thing, ask “what is this on Android?” Sometimes the answer was very close. Sometimes there was no answer at all.

What transferred

Dependency injection. If you have used Dagger or Hilt, Spring’s IoC container is not new. @Service and @Repository are like @Inject-able classes, @Configuration with @Bean methods is like a Hilt module with @Provides. Constructor injection is the recommended style in both.

The difference is when the wiring happens. Dagger generates code at compile time, so a missing dependency is a build error. Spring scans the classpath and builds the graph at startup with reflection and proxies, so a missing bean is a startup error. Both work. Spring is more flexible, Dagger tells you earlier.

HTTP, seen from the mirror. On Android I wrote Retrofit interfaces like this:

@GET("users/{id}")
Call<User> getUser(@Path("id") long id);

The Spring side is almost the same shape:

@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return userService.findById(id);
}

I already knew methods, headers, status codes and JSON. What changed is that now I choose them. Should creating a user return 200 or 201? What does a missing user return, 404 or an empty body? When I was the client, I complained about these choices. Now I had to make them.

Interceptors. An OkHttp Interceptor that adds an Authorization header has a mirror on the server: a filter that reads the header and checks the token. On Android I stored the JWT and attached it to every request. In Spring I wrote the other half: parse the token, verify it, reject the request if it is wrong. Spring Security is a chain of these filters. Once I saw it as “OkHttp interceptors, but on the receiving end”, it was much less scary.

Persistence. Room was my reference. MyBatis felt closest: you write the SQL yourself, in annotations or XML, and map the result to objects, like Room’s @Query. Spring Data JPA is further away. You declare findByName(String name) on an interface and the query is generated from the method name. It is convenient for simple queries and a bit magic for anything else.

The language. Java streams and Optional were easy after Kotlin’s collection functions and nullable types. Maven was new, but after years of Gradle the idea of a dependency tree and a parent version set was familiar.

What did not transfer

The threading model. This was the biggest change in how I think.

On Android there is one rule: don’t block the main thread. All my instincts are about moving work off one special thread.

On a server there is no special thread. In a classic Spring MVC app on Tomcat, each request is handled by one thread from a pool (200 by default). Blocking in a request is normal. You call the database and wait. The danger is somewhere else: many threads running the same code at the same time.

And by default, every Spring bean is a singleton. On Android a singleton holding mutable data already makes me nervous. On a server, one UserService instance is used by all request threads at once. So a field like this is a bug:

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private Order current; // shared by every request. Never do this.
}

Beans should be stateless. Per-request data goes in method parameters, or in a ThreadLocal. I used ThreadLocal to keep the current user after the JWT filter parsed the token, so the service layer can read it without passing it everywhere. But the threads are pooled and reused. If you don’t call remove() at the end of the request, the next request on that thread can see the previous user. On Android I almost never used ThreadLocal. Here it was in my notes in the first week, with a warning.

Transactions. Room has @Transaction, and I used it a few times. But on a phone there is one user, and the database is small and local. On a server, many users write the same tables at the same time, and a half-finished write can be seen by everyone.

@Transactional in Spring looks simple, but two details surprised me:

  • By default it rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error). A checked exception commits the transaction unless you say rollbackFor.
  • It works through a proxy. If a method in the same class calls another @Transactional method directly, the call does not go through the proxy, and the annotation on the inner method is ignored.

Both are easy to miss when you read the code, because the annotation is right there.

More than one copy of your app. An Android app runs once per phone. A backend service runs as several instances behind a load balancer. That changes many small decisions. You can’t keep a session in memory, because the next request may go to another instance. That is one reason tokens like JWT are popular: the server doesn’t need to remember anything. A cache like Redis sits outside the app so all instances share it.

I took some Spring Cloud notes back in 2023: service registry with Eureka and Nacos, load balancing, Feign clients, a gateway. At that time they were a list of names. This time, after thinking about “more than one copy”, I could see which problem each one solves. A registry answers “where are the other services”. A gateway is one door in front of many services. Feign makes a remote call look like an interface call, a bit like Retrofit between services.

Shipping. On Android, you upload a build to the store, the rollout is slow, and you watch crash reports. On a server, you build a jar, put it in a Docker image, and it is live in minutes. Logs, health checks and metrics are how you see it. The feedback is much faster, and so are the mistakes.

What I took away

  • Asking “what is this on Android?” gets you most of the way. DI, HTTP, interceptors and data mapping all have a close match.
  • The rest is about concurrency and scale. Shared singletons, pooled threads, transactions and many instances. My Android instincts had nothing to say there, and that is exactly the part to study slowly.
  • Being the client for years helps. I know what a confusing API feels like from the outside. Now I can try not to build one.
  • Annotations hide a lot. @Transactional, @Autowired, auto-configuration. Spring is easy to start because of them, and hard to debug for the same reason. Reading what they do underneath was the most useful part of these weeks.
